extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media watchdogs, scholars, and general readers interested in photojournalism ethics and media controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practices for assessing the trustworthiness, captioning, and editorial handling of news photographs (especially wartime/contested scenes). Includes detection of digital manipulation, staging, caption/timestamp verification, and institutional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deceptive digital manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Images must not be altered to misrepresent scenes; Adnan Hajj admitted using Photoshop to add and darken smoke spirals and to clone/duplicate elements so damage appeared worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of prohibited manipulation include adding smoke, duplicating flares/buildings, or cloning plumes. Reuters described this as 'photo editing software was improperly used on this image.' Anti-pattern: claiming edits were just to remove 'dust marks' when whole plumes/buildings were added. Detected manipulations led to removal of images and termination of relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial verification of freelance images
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations must verify photos supplied by freelancers before publication; Reuters stopped cooperation with the freelancer (Adnan Hajj) and removed his images after manipulations were discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial policy should explicitly prohibit altering pictures; agencies should investigate suspicious submissions, withdraw doctored content from archives/sales databases, and suspend or terminate relationships with photographers who breach policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: No staging or collusion with subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers and press tours must not stage scenes or collude with subjects to fabricate or dramatize events (e.g., Hezbollah operatives asking ambulances to switch on sirens for cameras).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of staged 'dog-and-pony show' press tours; report and investigate instances where rescue equipment or victims are manipulated for the camera. Distinguish between photographer complicity and use of journalists as tools by third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual plausibility and scrutiny of improbable details
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether image details are plausible in context (e.g., intact photographs or pristine albums lying undisturbed atop rubble, identical toys appearing across different scenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question recurring improbable elements that appear across multiple photographers/agencies; use common-sense forensic reasoning to flag likely fabrication or planting of props. CAMERA and critics cited the improbability of undisturbed photos on rubble as grounds for further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate captioning and timestamp integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions and timestamps must accurately reflect when, where, and what the photograph shows; inconsistencies (e.g., same subject appearing in photos with different times/captions) require correction and explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate time-stamp differences (feeds and websites may apply their own timestamps), ensure captions are corrected when errors are found (The New York Times issued a correction), and avoid implying causes or victim status without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain and examine original metadata and sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Original files, metadata and full photographic sequences should be preserved and examined to verify context and to resolve disputes about staging or authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single still frames can be misleading; checking the sequence of shots and original metadata helps confirm whether a subject was alive/dead, whether a scene was staged, or whether an element was added later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of independent forensic and technical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When image content relates to contested technical claims (e.g., type of munition or source of damage), independent forensic investigation and technical expertise should be used to assess the evidence (Human Rights Watch forensic report on ambulances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forensic reports may still be disputed; document methods, provide transparency about uncertainty (HRW's conclusions were challenged by critics), and avoid leaping to definitive causal claims without corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature public accusations based on limited evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make definitive accusations (of staging, fraud, or culpability) from single still images or isolated observations without corroboration; early critics (e.g., Taranto, Landes) later acknowledged mistakes after fuller review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corroborate with additional frames, eyewitness accounts, independent investigations, and technical analysis before publicly asserting staging or deception. Acknowledge uncertainty and correct the record when errors are discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical detection of digital tampering
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply technical methods (visual forensic inspection, pattern/clone detection) to identify signs of digital editing—bloggers identified Adobe Photoshop 'clone stamp' evidence and repeating patterns in doctored images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repeating patterns, duplicated buildings/plumes, inconsistent lighting/shadows, and other telltale artifacts. Public scrutiny and simple forensic checks can expose manipulations; publishers should perform such checks pre-publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections, transparency, and accountability by media organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Media outlets must publicly correct mistakes, explain errors, and take appropriate accountability measures (e.g., Reuters apologized, removed images, and an editor was later fired).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When manipulations or captioning errors are discovered, issue corrections, remove or relabel content as needed, disclose investigative findings, and apply disciplinary or remedial actions consistent with editorial policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographer responsibility for accurate captions and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers should provide accurate initial captions and update them when further investigation changes the understanding of a scene (Bruno Stevens amended his caption after further investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure captions reflect verified facts; if new information emerges that alters interpretation (e.g., whether a fire came from a downed jet or another source), correct captions and inform publishers of the changes.
